claims.text: Controlled annealing can induce local chemical ordering or nanoscale segregation in the selected high-entropy alloy.
The as-cast alloy has a random, chemically homogeneous configuration.
Annealing produces localized ordered or nanoscale-segregated regions within a generally disordered matrix.
Local chemical ordering increases the electronic density of states at specific lattice sites.
Local chemical ordering strengthens electron-phonon coupling.
The locally enhanced electron-phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation.
Cooper pairing is disrupted in the fully random as-cast state.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a detectable superconducting transition.
The superconducting transition will produce a sharp drop in electrical resistivity.
The superconducting transition will produce corresponding magnetic-susceptibility and heat-capacity features.
The annealed alloy's critical temperature will be detectable and either absent or significantly lower in the as-cast sample.
The as-cast baseline has no measurable superconducting transition or only a very weak superconducting response.
The hypothesis is intended to apply in a low-temperature window, described as typically below 40 K.
Ordering that is too weak to enhance electron-phonon coupling will not produce the predicted effect.
Macroscopic phase separation may place the material outside the proposed mechanism's regime of applicability.
Resistivity, magnetic susceptibility, heat capacity, and TEM can be used to compare superconducting behavior and local ordering between annealed and as-cast specimens.
A lack of a significant superconducting difference between annealed and as-cast samples is proposed as a falsifying outcome.
Failure of TEM to verify increased local ordering is proposed as a falsifying outcome.
